transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-01
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Evan Price (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam Chen (CTO - Mistral Payments), Sara Alvarez (Head of ML Ops), Owen Park (SRE)

Summary:
- Discovery focused on p95 latency SLOs, concurrency and streaming behaviour across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployments.
- Customer (Mistral Payments) needs sub-300ms p95 for short-turn responses for fraud-detection alerts, higher throughput during settlement windows.
- Action: run a 24h token/sec benchmark on hosted with customer prompt set; follow up tech deep dive.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency, streaming, batch vs single-token latency, token/sec benchmarking, KV/prefix caching, VPC/private deployment constraints, SOC2/audit logs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Evan from Redwood, AE on this account, and Priya is our SE. How's it going?
[00:07] Liam: Good, thanks. Time's tight, so we'll try to cover the p95 stuff and the concurrency profile.
[00:12] Priya: Great. Quick agenda: we want to understand your latency targets (p95), your concurrent streams, typical prompt lengths, and whether streaming is required. Then we can map to Hosted vs Dedicated sizing or Private.
[00:22] Sara: Yep. For fraud alerts, we need p95 around 200-300ms for short prompts — like 50-150 tokens — for the decision path. For longer context retrieval and reconciliation flows, latency can be higher, but throughput matters.
[00:36] Owen: And during settlement windows we might spike to 800-1000 concurrent requests for batch scoring; steady-state maybe 150 concurrent.
[00:44] Evan: Ok that's helpful. When you say p95 200-300ms, is that end-to-end including network + our app, or purely model generation?
[00:52] Liam: Ideally end-to-end, but we know network jitter will add ~30-50ms. So model p95 target is around 150-250ms.
[00:58] Priya: Understood. Few quick clarifying Qs: which models are you evaluating — open models, smaller quantized ones, or larger LLMs? And do you need streaming token-by-token responses?
[01:07] Sara: We're mostly on a mid-size open model family for production, leaning 7B-13B quantized in early stages. Streaming is important for UX on the fraud analyst dashboard — token streaming so we can start rendering.
[01:20] Evan: That maps well to Redwood Hosted for quick start; Dedicated if you want predictable SLOs and isolation; Private if you need customer-managed networking/KMS. Do you have compliance constraints?
[01:29] Liam: SOC 2 is required, plus enterprise KMS and VPC peering for production. We also need audit logs retained 1 year.
[01:37] Priya: We support SOC2, KMS integrations and audit retention — we'll share the security pack. URL in notes: https://redwood.example.com/security (note: auto-transcript sometimes drops chars).
[01:46] Owen: Can Redwood Dedicated hit that 150-250ms p95 for a 13B quantized model at 150 concurrent?
[01:55] Priya: Short answer: yes, but depends on prompt shapes and batching. Some constraints: continuous batching improves throughput but increases tail latency for single-shot short prompts. For p95 < 250ms we typically size for fewer concurrent streams per GPU and enable prefix/KV caching where applicable.
[02:13] Liam: Can you give an example numberset — tokens/sec and latency per GPU?
[02:17] Priya: Rough ballpark for a 13B quantized model on an A100-ish equivalent: single-stream generation (non-streaming) can do ~80-150 tokens/sec depending on decode settings. With streaming and smaller decode window, latency per token is ~10-20ms, but the p95 for completion of a 50-token prompt could still be in the 150-300ms range. For batching, you can push sustained token throughput to 1.5k-3k tokens/sec per GPU but that usually increases per-request p95 because of batch accumulation.
[02:48] Evan: So the tradeoff is clear: batch for cost but dedicated smaller batch windows or dedicated capacity for SLO.
[02:55] Sara: For us cost matters but SLA is critical — we can't let analyst-facing alerts be slow. We're considering a hybrid: Hosted for low-latency paths and Dedicated for bulk processing.
[03:06] Priya: That's a common setup. Practically, we recommend: Hosted (low latency, small volume), Dedicated reserved capacity for steady throughput, and Private only if you need on-prem/VPC for compliance. For your concurrency numbers (150 steady, 1k peak), we'd probably provision a small dedicated pool and use autoscale + burst capacity.
[03:23] Owen: And for streaming – does Redwood support immediate flush of early tokens to the client? Any buffering that could add to p95?
[03:31] Priya: Yes, we support token streaming. There is minimal buffering — sometimes the runtime accumulates a small decode window (a few tokens) to optimize perf. We can tune that to prioritize latency. There's also network serialization overhead; we measure token emit times in our console per-route.
[03:48] Liam: How do you measure p95? Do you provide dashboards and token-level breakdown?
[03:52] Evan: Redwood Console surfaces per-route p50/p95/p99, token-level cost, and breakdowns. We'll share an example dashboard screenshot.
[04:00] Sara: Good. For the benchmark we want you to run, we have two prompt types: short alert (avg 60 tokens, expect p95 <300ms) and long reconciliation (avg 800 tokens, p95 can be up to 2s). We'll share a sample prompt set.
[04:14] Priya: Perfect. For the short alerts we will run low-latency config: disable large batching windows, enable KV/prefix caching (if prompt repetition exists), and run with streaming enabled. For the long jobs we'll run high-throughput configuration.
[04:29] Owen: On the Dedicated side, what GPU instance types do you recommend? And what about quantization differences?
[04:35] Priya: We usually recommend 80GB-class GPUs for 13B with better perf (e.g., H100/A100 80GB). For cost we support 40GB with model sharding and quantization. Post-training 4-bit or 8-bit quantization results in different token/sec — 4-bit tends to increase throughput but can affect quality; we'll include quantization perf numbers in the follow-up.
[04:57] Liam: Any network topology gotchas for VPC peering, egress, or private deployments? We need <50ms network latency between our services and the model endpoint.
[05:06] Priya: For Private/VPC we deploy inside your VPC (or peer) and you manage routing. We recommend colocating in same region and using dedicated peering. We'll include recommended ip ranges and firewall rules in the security doc.
[05:20] Evan: Quick aside — competitors tend to promise low latency but often trade security or autoscale. Which ones are you considering?
[05:26] Liam: We're looking at VertexAI for tight cloud integration, Anthropic for evals, and also considering rolling our own with Triton.
[05:33] Priya: Rolling your own can be cheaper at scale but you take on kernel tuning and ops. Redwood tries to provide kernel selection, batching, and KV cache out-of-the-box.
[05:43] Sara: Can you talk through a sample sizing calc? If we want p95 <= 250ms for 150 concurrent short prompts, what does that look like?
[05:51] Priya: Rough sketch: assume each short prompt averages 60 tokens. If we target 150 concurrent single-shot requests and want low p95, we try to avoid large cross-request batching. That means roughly 150 active streams. If each GPU handles ~20-40 concurrent low-latency streams (varies), you'd need 4-8 GPUs. For sustained throughput spikes to 800-1k we rely on autoscale/burst — which could add extra GPUs for the window. We'll include a worked example in the follow-up.
[06:22] Owen: Those stream counts per GPU seem important — can you share observed concurrency vs latency curves?
[06:26] Priya: Yes, we'll attach a graph — in-house we've measured p95 jumps once concurrency per GPU goes above ~40 for low-latency configs on our 13B quantized profiles. There's also a model of diminishing returns with batching.
[06:40] Liam: Regarding token/sec benchmarks, how do you run reproducible tests? We need a 24h run with our real traffic shape.
[06:47] Evan: We'll run the Redwood benchmark harness. Process: you share prompt set and traffic distribution; we provision Hosted test env or spin Dedicated trial nodes; we run across a variety of concurrency levels and capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost.
[07:01] Sara: Can Hosted run with our KMS or do we need Dedicated/Private?
[07:05] Priya: Hosted uses Redwood-managed KMS by default; Dedicated/Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. For SOC2 plus customer KMS, Dedicated or Private is typical.
[07:16] Liam: Ok. Let's talk about a concrete benchmark scope now: short alerts at concurrency 150 steady, spike to 1k for 15 minutes; streaming on; token sizes 20-120. Long reconciliation: batched jobs 800 tokens average, 200 concurrent during batch windows.
[07:31] Priya: That is doable. We'll run two scenarios and capture p95, tokens/sec, and per-token cost. We will also log network and queuing delays.
[07:40] Evan: We'll need your sample prompt set and an API key or test credentials to reproduce exact behaviour on Hosted. Preferably a synthetic dataset without PII.
[07:48] Liam: We'll scrub and send the sample prompts — target by Monday.
[07:53] Sara: On the topic of token/sec, what's the expected cost delta between Hosted and Dedicated for this workload?
[07:59] Priya: Hosted has higher marginal unit price but no infra ops; Dedicated requires reservation which reduces per-token cost for sustained usage. We'll provide example cost calc showing break-even given your monthly token volume.
[08:10] Owen: For private deployment latency, do you expect any performance regress vs Dedicated?
[08:14] Priya: Private can match Dedicated if hardware equivalent; sometimes private on-prem can be slightly slower due to network or older GPUs. But if we ship the runtime tuned for your infra, performance is comparable.
[08:27] Liam: Any specific flags to enable low-latency at runtime? Like small batch windows, pre-warm KV cache?
[08:34] Priya: Yes: set batch_max_latency_ms low, set batch_max_tokens small, enable prefix/KV caching with TTL, and pin model instance warm threads. We can provide exact config snippets after the call.
[08:47] Evan: Priya, can you summarize the plan you propose for next week?
[08:50] Priya: Sure: 1) We'll run the 24h benchmark on Hosted with your prompt set on the 13B quantized profile, streaming enabled for short alerts. 2) We'll run a Dedicated-style test with similar instance types to simulate steady-state and spikes (autoscale). 3) Deliver p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost-per-token estimates, and config snippets.
[09:10] Liam: Good. A couple other questions: do you support per-route SLOs and automatic fallback to smaller models if load increases?
[09:16] Priya: Yes, we have smart routing and fallback policies — you can configure per-route model variants and fallback to a cheaper model or reduced token limit when latency SLOs are in danger.
[09:26] Sara: For audit logs and retention, is it easy to export logs to our SIEM?
[09:30] Evan: Yes, we support log export to S3, Splunk, and datadog — we can show sample retention configs.
[09:36] Owen: For the benchmark, will you include a breakdown of per-token time: kernel time vs scheduling vs network?
[09:42] Priya: We'll include as much as the runtime exposes — e.g., kernel time, decode time, batch wait time, and network emit time. There are cases where proper attribution is fuzzy but we'll be transparent.
[09:54] Liam: One potential concern: in-house we saw tail latency spikes due to KV cache thrash when contexts are large and unique. How do you mitigate that?
[10:02] Priya: We have eviction strategies, segmented KV caches per-tenant, and can tune cache TTL vs memory. Also we can recommend prompt engineering to increase prefix reuse where possible.
[10:12] Sara: About encryption — do you support encrypt-at-rest for cache?
[10:16] Priya: Yes, encryption at rest is standard; with Dedicated/Private you can plug in your KMS.
[10:21] Evan: Anything else from the customer?
[10:23] Owen: Not yet. We'll await the benchmark plan and send prompts.
[10:27] Liam: Quick follow-up: if results look promising, what's typical lead time to get Dedicated capacity live?
[10:33] Evan: Usually 2-4 weeks depending on contract and capacity availability — we can prioritize based on your timeline.
[10:39] Sara: Ok, we'll aim for a pilot in 3 weeks if benchmarks are good.
[10:44] Evan: Great. I'll capture action items.
[10:47] Priya: I'll own the benchmark runs and make sure to include per-route dashboard links and config snippets.
[10:54] Liam: Thanks everyone.
[10:56] Evan: Thanks — we will follow up with the security pack and pricing.
